summary.text: For \(n=473165\), the intermediate integer \(5292270077783=a(n)+4\) lies strictly between the two endpoints.  It is a Sierpiński number because a period-48 covering congruence shows that, for every positive exponent \(m\), one of \(3,5,7,17,97,257,673\) divides \(5292270077783\cdot2^m+1\), which is larger than all these divisors and hence composite.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=9454129+11184810n.
\]
Recall that a Sierpiński number is an odd integer \(k>1\) such that, for every positive integer \(m\), the number \(k2^m+1\) is not prime.

We disprove the proposed assertion by taking
\[
n_0=473165.
\]
A direct calculation gives
\[
11184810\cdot473165=5292260623650,
\]
and hence
\[
a(n_0)=9454129+5292260623650=5292270077779.
\]
Now put
\[
K=5292270077783.
\]
Thus
\[
K=a(n_0)+4.
\]
In particular,
\[
a(n_0)<K<a(n_0)+28,
\]
since \(0<4<28\). It remains to prove that \(K\) is itself a Sierpiński number. This will exhibit a Sierpiński number strictly between the two allegedly consecutive ones.

We prove the Sierpiński property of \(K\) using a covering system of period \(48\). First note the factorization
\[
2^{48}-1
 =281474976710655
 =3^2\cdot5\cdot7\cdot13\cdot17\cdot97\cdot241\cdot257\cdot673.
\]
Consequently,
\[
2^{48}\equiv1\pmod p
\]
for every
\[
p\in\{3,5,7,17,97,257,673\}.
\]
Therefore, if \(m=48q+r\), where \(0\le r<48\), then for each such \(p\),
\[
2^m=2^{48q+r}=(2^{48})^q2^r\equiv2^r\pmod p.
\]
Thus divisibility of \(K2^m+1\) can be decided solely from the residue \(r=m\bmod48\).

The required covering congruences are given in the following table. Each row specifies a set of possible residues \(r\), a divisor \(p\), the residue of \(K\) modulo \(p\), and the corresponding residue of \(2^r\) modulo \(p\):

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
 r & p & K\pmod p & 2^r\pmod p\\ \hline
0,2,4,\ldots,46 & 3 & 2 & 1\\
1,13,25,37 & 7 & 3 & 2\\
3,7,11,15,19,23,27,31,35,39,43,47 & 5 & 3 & 3\\
5,21 & 257 & 8 & 32\\
9,17,33,41 & 17 & 8 & 2\\
29 & 97 & 94 & 65\\
45 & 673 & 665 & 589
\end{array}
\]

For completeness, the stated residues of \(K\) follow from the integer divisions
\[
\begin{aligned}
K&=3(1764090025927)+2,\\
K&=5(1058454015556)+3,\\
K&=7(756038582540)+3,\\
K&=17(311310004575)+8,\\
K&=97(54559485337)+94,\\
K&=257(20592490575)+8,\\
K&=673(7863699966)+665.
\end{aligned}
\]
The entries for \(2^r\) are elementary modular exponentiations. Their repeated patterns can also be seen directly: modulo \(3\), every even power of \(2\) is \(1\); modulo \(5\), all exponents \(r\equiv3\pmod4\) give \(2^r\equiv3\); modulo \(7\), the exponents \(1,13,25,37\), all congruent to \(1\pmod{12}\), give \(2^r\equiv2\). The remaining finite values are
\[
2^5\equiv2^{21}\equiv32\pmod{257},
\]
\[
2^9\equiv2^{17}\equiv2^{33}\equiv2^{41}\equiv2\pmod{17},
\]
\[
2^{29}\equiv65\pmod{97},
\qquad
2^{45}\equiv589\pmod{673}.
\]

In every row, multiplying the last two columns and adding \(1\) produces a multiple of the indicated \(p\):
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
p& (K\bmod p)(2^r\bmod p)+1\\ \hline
3&2\cdot1+1=3\\
7&3\cdot2+1=7\\
5&3\cdot3+1=10=2\cdot5\\
257&8\cdot32+1=257\\
17&8\cdot2+1=17\\
97&94\cdot65+1=6111=63\cdot97\\
673&665\cdot589+1=391686=582\cdot673.
\end{array}
\]
It follows that, whenever \(r\) belongs to a row of the table,
\[
K2^r+1\equiv0\pmod p.
\]
Together with \(2^m\equiv2^r\pmod p\), this gives
\[
p\mid K2^m+1.
\]

It remains only to check that the table covers every possible residue modulo \(48\). The first row contains all \(24\) even residues. Among the odd residues, the third row contains precisely the \(12\) residues congruent to \(3\pmod4\). The remaining twelve residues, which are all congruent to \(1\pmod4\), are
\[
1,5,9,13,17,21,25,29,33,37,41,45.
\]
They are partitioned as
\[
\{1,13,25,37\},\quad
\{5,21\},\quad
\{9,17,33,41\},\quad
\{29\},\quad
\{45\},
\]
which are exactly the residue sets in the rows for \(7,257,17,97,673\), respectively. Hence every integer \(m\) falls into one and only one of the displayed covering cases.

Now let \(m>0\). By the covering just proved, \(K2^m+1\) has a divisor
\[
p\in\{3,5,7,17,97,257,673\}.
\]
Every such \(p\) is greater than \(1\). Moreover,
\[
K2^m+1>K>673\ge p,
\]
so \(p\) is a proper divisor of \(K2^m+1\). Therefore \(K2^m+1\) is not prime. Since this holds for every positive \(m\), the required universal non-primality condition is satisfied.

Finally, \(K=5292270077783\) is odd—its last digit is \(3\)—and plainly \(K>1\). Thus \(K\) is a Sierpiński number.

We have therefore found, at \(n=473165\), the strict inequalities
\[
a(473165)=5292270077779
<5292270077783
<5292270077807=a(473165)+28,
\]
with the middle number \(5292270077783\) a Sierpiński number. Hence \(a(473165)\) and \(a(473165)+28\) cannot be consecutive Sierpiński numbers. This single counterexample disproves the assertion that they are consecutive for every \(n\ge0\).
